overview: Discounted cash flow is the bedrock identity of fixed income: a bond is nothing but its cash flows, and a cash flow tomorrow is worth its amount times the price of money for that date. The zero curve *is* that price list — one discount factor per date — so pricing reduces to reading factors off the curve and summing. Everything subtle in bond-land (accrued interest, clean versus dirty, yield conventions) is bookkeeping layered on top of this one idea.
formula_latex: P_{dirty} = \sum_{i} CF_i \cdot DF(t_i), \qquad P_{clean} = P_{dirty} - AI

variables.name: Cash flows
variables.why_it_matters: The contract itself: coupons of F·c/m at each schedule date plus the face value at maturity. DCF takes them as certain — which is exactly the assumption credit models later relax.

variables.name: Discount factors
variables.why_it_matters: The market's exchange rate between money now and money at t. Read off the zero curve; every rates product in this laboratory ultimately prices off these same factors, which is why one consistent curve matters more than any single formula.

variables.name: Accrued interest
variables.why_it_matters: The seller earned part of the current coupon by holding the bond since the last payment. Quoted (clean) prices exclude it so that prices don't saw-tooth on coupon dates; the buyer nevertheless pays dirty.

variables.name: Yield to maturity
variables.why_it_matters: The single rate, compounded at the coupon frequency, that reprices the bond exactly. Not an input here but an *output* — a convenient one-number summary of the whole curve's effect on this bond, and the axis on which duration and convexity live.

assumptions: Cash flows are certain: no default, no prepayment, no embedded options.
The zero curve fully describes the time value of money for this issuer's currency.
Discount factors between pillar dates follow the curve's interpolation (log-linear in DF here).
The bond can be valued in isolation — no liquidity or financing frictions.
limitations: Silently ignores credit: a corporate bond discounted on the risk-free curve is overpriced. In practice a spread is added — which is a model extension, not a fix within DCF.
Cannot see optionality. A callable bond's issuer will refinance when rates fall; plain DCF prices the bond as if they never will, and therefore overvalues it exactly when the call bites.
Only as good as the curve: interpolation choices and stale pillars flow straight into price.
Duration/convexity summaries assume parallel yield moves; real curves twist and steepen.
when_to_use: Any instrument that is genuinely a fixed schedule of cash flows: bullet government bonds, zero coupons, swap legs, annuity streams. Also as the base layer other models extend.
when_not_to_use: Anything contingent — callable/puttable bonds, caps and floors, options — or credit-risky debt without a spread adjustment. Those need trees, closed forms, or hazard-rate models built on top of the same discounting machinery.
industry_usage: Universal. Every rates desk, treasury system, and risk engine begins with curve-based discounting; the argument is only ever about which curve and which adjustments.
computational_complexity: O(n) in the number of cash flows — effectively free.
